blocks.text: The Annual National Government Budget Implementation Review Report for FY 2022/23 covers 1st July 2022 to 30th June 2023. It has been prepared in fulfilment of Article 228 of the Constitution of Kenya and Section 9 of the Controller of Budget Act, 2016, which require the COB to submit quarterly budget implementation reports for the National and County governments to Parliament.

The reporting period is primarily defined by a transition in government and recovery from the adverse effects of the COVID-19 pandemic. Upon taking office, the new administration instituted measures to rationalise expenditure on non-core activities, reduce deficit financing, and enhance funding for development activities. On the other hand, economic policies and programs that cushioned citizens and businesses from the adverse impact of the pandemic were sustained to build on the progress realised in returning the economy to a more sustainable growth path for improved livelihoods.

The revised gross budget for both National and County Governments for FY 2022/23 amounted to Kshs.4.18 trillion, comprising Kshs.3.67 trillion for the National Government and Kshs.515.18 billion for the forty-seven County Governments. The National Government budget consisted of Kshs.584.29 billion for ministerial development expenditure, Kshs.3.09 trillion for recurrent expenditure (Kshs.1.51 trillion for recurrent ministerial expenditure and Kshs.1.58 trillion for Consolidated Fund Services (CFS).

Receipts into the Consolidated Fund amounted to Kshs.3.24 trillion, representing 89.6 per cent of the revised net estimates of Kshs.3.62 trillion. The total exchequer issues from the Consolidated Fund to MDAs, CFS and County Governments amounted to Kshs.3.24 trillion, representing 89.6 per cent of the revised net estimates, a decrease compared to 89.9 per cent recorded in FY 2021/22. The total expenditure by the National Government amounted to Kshs.3.18 trillion, representing 86.6 per cent of the revised gross estimates, an increase compared to 85.4 per cent (Kshs.3.0 trillion) recorded in FY 2021/22. The expenditure comprised ministerial development expenditure at Kshs.473.55 billion (absorption rate of 81.0 per cent), recurrent ministerial expenditure at Kshs.1.40 trillion (absorption rate of 92.8 per cent), CFS at Kshs.1.31 trillion (82.7 per cent), and gross expenditure for County governments amounting to Kshs.428.90 billion (83.6 per cent).

Development expenditure recorded a 14.4 per cent decline compared to Kshs.553.37 billion spent in FY 2021/22. The highest development expenditure categories included; capital transfers by the MDAs at Kshs.345.09 billion, followed by construction and civil works at Kshs.25.17 billion, representing 72.9 per cent and 5.3 per cent of the gross development expenditure, respectively.

A review of the recurrent expenditure shows that Kshs.551.44 billion was spent on Grants, and Kshs.542.46 billion 1 was spent on Compensation to Employees, representing 39.4 per cent and 38.7 per cent of the gross recurrent expenditure by MDAs. Subsidies totalled Kshs.127.72 billion, representing 9.1 per cent of the recurrent expenditure, while use of goods and services amounted to Kshs.94.44 billion representing 6.7 per cent of recurrent expenses.
The Public debt stock recorded 18.8 per cent growth from Kshs.8.63 trillion reported on 30th June 2022 to Kshs.10.25 trillion as of 30 th June 2023, attributed to loan disbursements and weakening of

the Kenyan Shilling. The public debt stock comprises Kshs.4.83 trillion from domestic lenders and Kshs.5.42 trillion from external lenders. The allocation for servicing public debt was Kshs.1.39 trillion in the approved Supplementary Budget II, while cumulative expenditure on public debt in FY 2022/23 amounted to Kshs.1.15 trillion, representing 83.3 per cent of the annual allocation.

The Controller of Budget identified vital challenges that hindered effective budget implementation in FY 2022/23. They included: an increase in the public debt leading to a rise in the country's debt service costs, thereby limiting the government's fiscal space to undertake other critical policies and programmes; liquidity constraints arising from investors' preference for the shorter 91-day Treasury Bills; the establishment of a Special Committee on the verification of pending bills by the Cabinet on 27 th June 2023 did not include critical institutions in public finance management such as the Controller of Budget, Office of the Auditor General, the National Treasury and County Treasuries. Further, several MDAs' economic items and sub-programmes exceeded their allocated budget and reflected negative balances.

To address the challenges, the Controller of Budget recommends a special audit of the existing loans and committed loans to link each loan to the funded project; the National Treasury should explore opportunities of accessing funding in multiple currencies to hedge against intense pressure on the local currency; fiscal consolidation to ensure budgetary discipline; consideration to include key players in public finance management in the pending bills verification committee as key stakeholders in the implementation of the budget; and finally, Accounting Officer should adhere to Section 43 of the PFM Act and ensure reallocated budget items are regularised in the consequent supplementary budget.

The Office of the Controller of Budget (OCoB) is an independent office established under Article 228 of the Constitution of Kenya. Its primary mandate is to oversee the implementation of the budget for the National and County governments by authorising withdrawals from Public Funds under Articles 204, 206, and 207 of the Constitution and to report on the implementation of the budgets to each House of Parliament every four months. The report is in line with Section 9(5) of the COB Act 2016, which states that despite the first quarterly report of the year submitted under Section 9, each subsequent report shall contain cumulative amounts from the beginning of that year.

In the analysis of the budget performance, the MDAs are classified into ten sectors, according to the United Nations Classification of the Functions of the Government, including (i) Agriculture, Rural and Urban Development (ARUD), (ii) Education, (iii) Energy, Infrastructure, and Information Communications Technology, (iv) Environmental Protection, Water and Natural Resources, (v) General Economic and Commercial Affairs, (vi) Governance, Justice, Law and Order, (vii) Health, (viii) National Security, (ix) Public Administration and International Relations, (x) Social Protection, Culture, and Recreation, sector.

The report is presented in six chapters. Chapter One is the introduction. Chapter Two presents receipts into the Consolidated Fund and actual withdrawals from the Consolidated Fund to fund expenditures for the Consolidated Fund Services, Development budget, Recurrent Budget and the equitable shareable revenue to County governments. The National government budget comprises gross and net estimates; the difference is referred to as Appropriation-In-Aid (A-I-A). A-I-A may be loans, grants from development partners and fees/levies for services rendered by MDAs and are used to defray expenses. Net Estimate is the proportion of budget funded through the exchequer by the National Treasury, and its performance is based on the proportion issued over the net estimates.

Chapter Three presents a summary of budget performance, the status of pending bills for the National and County governments, and MDAs' expenditure by economic classification disaggregated into development and recurrent votes. In addition, it presents Consolidated Fund Services performance, which includes Public debt, Salaries, allowances and Miscellaneous Services and Pensions and gratuity.

Chapter Four presents the budget performance of MDAs in each of the ten sectors. The absorption rate is the proportion of expenditure to the gross budget and expresses the implementation percentage of the budget in the financial year. The budget performance reflects the MDAs' expenditure, deliverables by programmes and sub-programmes, both financial and non-financial and major ongoing projects completion status.

Chapter Five presents the key issues identified by the Controller of Budget as inhibitors of effective budget implementation in FY 2022/23. Appropriate recommendations are included to address the problems identified.

Chapter Six provides the report's conclusion. Annexes support the chapters. Annex I presents a summary of MDAs' development expenditure, Annex II presents MDAs' recurrent expenditure, Annex III shows MDAs' development expenditure by sector, Annex IV shows MDAs' recurrent spending by sector, Annex V shows MDAs' total expenditure by sector, Annex VI shows Capital Transfer to SAGAs,

Annex VII shows Current Transfer to SAGAs, Annex VIII shows MDAS pending bills for FY 2022/23 as of 31st June 2023, Annex IX shows State Corporations/State Owned Enterprises/SAGAS pending bills for FY 2022/23 as of 31st June 2023, Annex X displays County Governments Pending Bills For FY 2022/23 as of 30 th June 2023. Annex XI shows a summary of compensation to employees paid through IPPD compared to IFMIS payment.

2.2 Revenue Estimates and Receipts into the Consolidated Fund
heading_path: 2.2 Revenue Estimates and Receipts into the Consolidated Fund

blocks.text: This section presents a summary of receipts into the Consolidated Fund for FY 2022/23. The Consolidated Fund is established under Article 206(1) of the Constitution of Kenya and refers to the account into which all money raised or received by or on behalf of the National government is paid. However, it excludes monies reasonably excluded by an Act of Parliament and payable into other public funds established for a specific purpose or is retained by the State organ that received it to defray its expenses.
heading_path: 2.2 Revenue Estimates and Receipts into the Consolidated Fund

blocks.text: The original revenue estimate for FY 2022/23 was Kshs.3.54 trillion, revised to Kshs.3.61 trillion in Supplementary Budget I and to Kshs.3.62 trillion in Supplementary Budget II compared to Kshs.3.33 trillion (revised), allocated in FY 2021/22, representing 1.6 per cent growth (Kshs.0.06 billion). To finance the budget, the government budgeted to raise revenue from Tax Revenue (Kshs.2.08 trillion), Non-Tax Revenue (Kshs.65.56 billion), Domestic Borrowing (Kshs.948.11 billion), External Loans and Grants (Kshs.513.42 billion) and Other Domestic Financing (Kshs.13.23 billion).

The specific revenue categories projected to grow were Tax Revenue by 0.4 per cent (Kshs.7.91 billion) and External Loans and Grants by 47 per cent (Kshs.164.09 billion). Non-Tax Revenue, Other Domestic Financing and Domestic borrowing reduced by 5.9 per cent (Kshs.4.1 billion) and 8.9 per cent (Kshs.92.35 billion), respectively.

In FY 2022/23, actual receipts into the Consolidated Fund amounted to Kshs.3.24 trillion, representing 89.6 per cent of the annual target, compared to Kshs.3.06 trillion (91.7 per cent of the annual target) recorded in FY 2021/22. The receipts comprised opening balances from the previous financial year (FY 2021/22), Tax and Non-Tax Revenue, Domestic borrowing, External Loans and Grants, and Other Domestic Financing. Trend analysis shows a 6.1 per cent growth in receipts in FY 2022/23 compared to a similar period in FY 2021/22. This is mainly attributed to External Loans and Grants growth from Kshs.239.61 billion received in FY 2021/22 to Kshs.488.31 billion received in FY 2022/23 (an increase of Kshs.248.7 billion). In addition, tax revenue recorded an increase of Kshs.122.50 billion compared to Kshs.1,784.39 billion received in FY 2021/22. Further, as shown in Table 2.1, Non-Tax Revenue had the highest performance against the annual target of 125.1 per cent, followed by Other Domestic Financing at 121.7 per cent. On the other hand, Domestic Borrowing had the lowest performance of 73.5 per cent against its annual target, i.e. it dropped by Kshs.180.64 billion from Kshs.877.04 billion received in FY 2021/22.

The approved gross budget for FY 2022/23 amounted to Kshs.4.19 trillion, revised to Kshs.4.18 trillion after budget revisions. The original budget comprised Kshs.715.35 billion for development expenditure and was revised to Kshs.618.16 billion in Supplementary Budget I and Kshs.582.24 billion in Supplementary Budget II, Kshs.2.97 trillion for recurrent expenditure adjusted to Kshs.3.05 trillion in Supplementary Budget I and Kshs.3.09 trillion in Supplementary Budget II, and Kshs.515.18 billion to County Governments including Kshs.399.6 billion as shareable revenue from the National government. The revised budget represented a 4.6 per cent (Kshs.185.3 billion) increase compared to the Kshs.4 trillion approved in FY 2020/21

blocks.text: MDAs are classified into ten sectors according to the United Nations Classification of Functions of Government, designed to support fiscal analysis by breaking down Government Financial Statistics for comparability across sectors. The ten sectors include (i) Agriculture, Rural and Urban Development (ARUD), (ii) Education, (iii) Energy, Infrastructure, and Information Communications Technology,

(iv) Environmental Protection, Water and Natural Resources, (v) General Economic and Commercial Affairs, (vi) Governance, Justice, Law and Order, (vii) Health, (viii) National Security, (ix) Public Administration and International Relations, (x) Social Protection, Culture, and Recreation, sector. The Education sector received the highest proportion of exchequer issues to revised net estimates at 97.9 per cent a similar proportion as compared to FY 2021/22. The General Economic and Commercial Affairs sector received the lowest exchequer issues at 84.2 per cent a drop of 9.1 per cent from the 93.3 per cent exchequer disbursement to net estimates in FY 2021/22.

In FY 2022/23, gross allocation to the development budget was Kshs.715.35 billion, revised to Kshs.618.16 billion in Supplementary Budget I, and Kshs.582.24 billion in Supplementary Budget II representing 15.9 per cent of the National Government budget of Kshs.3.67 trillion and 27.9 per cent of ministerial allocation (Kshs.2.09 trillion). Sectors whose percentage of exchequer issues to revised net estimates declined between FY 2022/23 and FY 2021/22 include the National Security Sector (a drop of 48.1 per cent), GECA Sector (a drop of 20.1 per cent), SPCR Sector (a drop of 16.2 per cent) and ARUD Sector (a drop of 9.6 per cent).

blocks.text: The Equalisation Fund is established under Article 204 (1) of the Constitution of Kenya, which requires that half a per cent (0.5 per cent) of all the revenue collected by the National government each year, calculated based on the most recent audited revenue received, as approved by the National Assembly, to

be paid into the Fund. Article 204(2) of the Constitution provides that the National Government shall use the Equalisation Fund only to provide essential services, including Water, Roads, Health Facilities, and Electricity to marginalised areas to the extent necessary to bring the quality of those services in those areas to the level generally enjoyed by the rest of the nation, so far as is possible.

In the FY 2022/23, the Controller of Budget authorised Kshs.670.35 million from the Equalization Fund comprising Kshs.567.85 million for development expenditure for pending bills projects implemented by the State Department for Water, Sanitation and Irrigation, and Kshs.102.5 million related to Equalization Fund Secretariat expenses. This chapter presents the overall budget performance in FY 2022/23 for the National and County Governments, comprising development and recurrent expenditure. National government recurrent consists of Ministerial expenditure and Consolidated Fund Services. CFS comprises Public debt, Pensions, and Gratuities, as well as Salaries and Allowances to Constitutional Office holders and Miscellaneous services. The chapter also presents the budget performance by economic classification for the development and recurrent votes for MDAs. In addition, it presents pending bills status as of 30th June 2023.

The approved gross budget for both National and County Governments for the FY 2022/23 amounted to Kshs.4.19 trillion, revised to Kshs.4.18 trillion in Supplementary Budget I, and Kshs.4.18 trillion in Supplementary Budget II, presenting 4.6 per cent growth compared to Kshs.4 trillion in a similar period in FY 2021/22. This comprised Kshs.715.35 billion for MDAs' development expenditure revised to Kshs.618.16 billion in Supplementary Budget I, and Kshs.582.24 trillion in Supplementary Budget II, (see Annex I, referenced on page 131) , Kshs.1.40 trillion for MDAs' recurrent revised to Kshs.1.50 trillion in the Supplementary Budget I, and Kshs.1.51 trillion in Supplementary Budget II, ( see Annex II, referenced on page 134 , Kshs.1.57 trillion for CFS revised to Kshs.1.55 trillion in the Supplementary Budget I, and Kshs.1.58 trillion in Supplementary Budget II, and Kshs.515.18 billion cumulative County Governments Budget that includes the equitable share of Kshs.399.6 billion.

The MDAs' Development and County budgets recorded a decline of 15.2 per cent and 3.8 per cent compared to Kshs.688.75 billion and Kshs.535.74 billion recorded in a similar period FY 2021/2. In contrast, the MDAs' recurrent and CFS allocation recorded growth of 3.1 per cent and 20.5 per cent compared FY 2021/22 allocations of Kshs.1.46 trillion and Kshs.1.31 trillion, respectively.

The government targeted to finance the budget through revenue of Kshs.2.15 trillion revised to Kshs.2.21 trillion in Supplementary Budget I, and Kshs.2.16 trillion in Supplementary Budget II, which comprises tax revenue of Kshs.2.08 trillion, non-tax revenue of Kshs.65.56 billion, and other domestic financings of Kshs.13.23 billion. The budget was also to be financed by domestic borrowing of Kshs.1.46 trillion, which comprises net domestic borrowing of Kshs.480.42 billion and internal debt redemptions (roll-overs) of Kshs.467.69 billion. Further, the budget was to be financed by external loans and grants amounting to Kshs.513.42 billion.

The County governments targeted to finance their budget(s) byKshs.370.00 billion as the equitable share of revenue raised Nationally, generate Kshs.57.37 billion from own revenue sources, utilise Kshs.42.03 billion cash balance from FY 2021/22 (including Kshs.29.60 billion balance as at 30th June 2022 equitable share) and Kshs.22.52 billion as conditional grants (Kshs.5.36 billion and Kshs.17.16 billion from national government and development partners respectively).

The total funding by the National Treasury and County Treasuries in FY 2022/23 was Kshs.3.27 trillion, representing 87.6 per cent of the revised net estimates, compared to 89.9 per cent (Kshs.3.15 trillion) recorded in a similar period FY 2021/22. The exchequer issues comprised Kshs.308.03 billion (82.4 per cent) for MDAs' development expenditure, Kshs.1.22 trillion for recurrent MDAs' expenditure (96.3 per cent), Kshs.1.31 trillion to CFS (83.3 per cent) and Kshs.430.48 billion for the County Governments (83.6 per cent). The National and County governments' gross expenditure was Kshs.3.61 trillion, recording an absorption rate of 86.2 per cent, compared to 83.9 per cent (Kshs.3.36 trillion) recorded in FY 2021/22.

National Government gross expenditure amounts to Kshs.3.18 trillion, representing 86.6 per cent of the revised gross estimate, comprising MDAs' development expenditure at Kshs.473.55 billion (absorption rate of 81.0 per cent), recurrent MDAs' expenditure at Kshs.1.4 trillion (absorption rate of 92.8 per cent) and Consolidated Fund Services at Kshs.1.31 trillion (82.7 per cent). Gross expenditure for County governments amounted to Kshs.428.90 billion, recording an absorption rate of 83.3 per cent, compared to Kshs.400.96 billion (74.8 per cent) recorded in FY 2021/22. This comprised development expenditure amounting to Kshs.97.98 billion (absorption rate of 61.0 per cent) and recurrent expenditure at Kshs.330.92 billion (recording an absorption rate of 93.3 per cent). The CFS comprises funds allocated towards (i) Repayment of Public Debt (domestic and foreign) and government-guaranteed loans to parastatals, (ii) Pensions and Gratuities, (iii) Salaries and Allowances to Constitutional Officeholders and Miscellaneous Services, and (iv) Subscriptions to International Organisations.

In  the  FY  2022/23,  the  CFS  was  allocated  Kshs.1.57  trillion,  revised  to  Kshs.1.55  trillion  in Supplementary Budget I and Kshs1.58 trillion in Supplementary Budget II recording 20.5 per cent growth (Kshs.268.26 billion) compared to Kshs.1.31 trillion allocated in FY 2021/22. The growth is attributed to additional budget on all the CFS categories with Salaries, Allowances and Miscellaneous recording the highest proportion, above 100 per cent as shown in Table 3.2.

A review of CFS allocation in FY 2022/23 shows that public debt recorded Kshs.10.3 billion growth from Kshs.1.57 trillion in the printed estimates to Kshs1.58 trillion in the revised estimates (supplementary II), representing 0.7 per cent increase, attributed to an increase in allocation towards external loan interest payments and payment of Guaranteed Debt to bail-out Kenya Airways. Allocation towards external loan interest payments recorded the highest increment of Kshs17.7 billion recording 12.9 per cent growth from Kshs.137.24 billion in the printed estimates to Kshs.154.94 billion in the revised estimates (Supplementary II). Allocation towards internal borrowing interest payment declined by Kshs.21.08 billion (3.8 per cent) from Kshs.549.01 billion allocations in the printed estimates to Kshs.527.93 billion in the revised estimates.

Domestic debt interest comprises government overdraft interest charges by CBK, Pre-1997 government overdraft debt, Short-Term Borrowing (Treasury Bill's interest), miscellaneous (advertising cost), interest on bonds and other loans, and commission to CBK.

The overdraft facility is a temporary source of cash to manage cash flow which is administered by the Central Bank of Kenya (CBK) and is restricted to a maximum of five per cent of the most recently audited revenues. It is expected to be paid off by the end of the financial year as specified in Section 15 (3) of the PFM Act.

The overdraft limit for FY 2022/23 was raised to Kshs.80 billion from Kshs.75 billion in FY 2021/22. In the FY 2022/23, the budgeted overdraft interest charge was Kshs.5.28 billion whose actual charge was Kshs.5.16 billion. Table 3.6 shows monthly overdraft charges from July 2022 to June 2023.

blocks.text: MDAs are classified into ten sectors according to the United Nation Classification of Functions of Government, which is designed to support fiscal analysis by breaking down Government Fiscal Statistics for comparability. The chapter presents the performance of MDAs by sector in FY 2022/23 (see Annex III to Annex V, referenced on page 140 to page142). It provides budget allocations per sector detailing specific MDAs' exchequer issues, expenditures, and absorption on the budget. The chapter also presents the performance of MDAs' programmes and sub-programmes, key achievements and spending on development projects in FY 2022/23.

Sector performance is presented in alphabetical order as follows; (i) Agriculture, Rural and Urban Development (ARUD), (ii) Education, (iii) Energy, Infrastructure and Information Communications Technology (EI & ICT), (iv) Environment Protection, Water and Natural Resources (EWNR) (v) General Economic and Commercial Affairs (GECA) (vi) Governance, Justice, Law, and Order (GJLO) (vii) Health (viii) National Security (ix) Public Administration and International Relations (PAIR) (x) Social Protection, Culture and Recreation (SPCR) Sectors.

In FY 2022/23, the Education sector was allocated Kshs.568.22 billion (27.1 per cent of the total MDAs gross allocation of Kshs.2.09 trillion), recording the highest budget allocation while the GECA sector was allocated Kshs.29.08 billion (1.4 per cent), representing the lowest budgetary allocation. The allocation to the Education sector is skewed towards recurrent at Kshs.534.21 billion (94.0 per cent of the Sector's Budget) and development allocation of Kshs.34.02 billion (6.0 per cent of the Sector's Budget).

In the FY 2022/23 the development budget was revised from Kshs.715.35 billion to Kshs.618.16 billion and Kshs.584.29 billion in Supplementary Budget I and II respectively representing 8.6 per cent decline. The Ministerial recurrent budget was revised from Kshs.1.40 trillion to Kshs.1.50 trillion and to Kshs.1.51 trillion in Supplementary I & II representing 7 per cent growth.
4.2 Agriculture, Rural and Urban Development (ARUD) Sector
heading_path: 4.2 Agriculture, Rural and Urban Development (ARUD) Sector

blocks.text: Agriculture is a devolved function under the Fourth Schedule of the Constitution of Kenya. It is a critical sector in the economic pillar of the Kenya Vision 2030.

The sector consists of six MDAs, namely: Ministry of Lands and Physical Planning, the State Department for Crop Development and Agricultural Research, the State Department for Livestock, the State Department for Fisheries, Aquaculture and the Blue Economy, the State Department for Cooperatives, and the National Land Commission (NLC), together with affiliated Semi-Autonomous Government Agencies and Training Institutions.

The overall goal of the sector is to attain National food and nutritional security and sustainable fisheries and land management, co-operatives growth, and the blue economy's utilization. Kenya's economic blueprint, the Kenya Vision 2030, and the Government Agenda on the 'Big Four' economic strategy both recognise the ARUD sector as a critical player in the economic and social development of the
country through food production, employment and wealth creation, foreign exchange earnings, security of land tenure and land management.

The allocation to the ARUD sector represents 2.6 per cent of the revised gross National budget. The budget comprised Kshs.66.61 billion (70.7 per cent) for development activities and Kshs.27.55 billion (29.7 per cent) for recurrent expenditure. The State Department for Crop Development and Agricultural Research received the highest budgetary allocation at Kshs.49.42 billion (52.5 per cent of the ARUD sector's budget), while the National Land Commission had the lowest budgetary allocation at Kshs.1.48 billion (1.6 per cent of the ARUD Sector allocation).

blocks.text: The Education Sector comprises six MDAs: The State Department for Early Learning and Basic Education, the State Department for University Education and Research, the State Department for Vocational and Technical Training, the State Department for Post-Training and Skills Development, the State Department for Implementation of Curriculum Reforms, and Teachers Service Commission (TSC) together with their affiliated Agencies and Institutions.

The Education sector is critical in promoting Kenya's political, social, and economic development by developing all-around individuals who can overcome prevailing societal challenges. The sector envisions attaining quality and inclusive education, training, and research for sustainable development. The Education sector is committed to providing quality education, training, science, technology, research, and skills development to all Kenyans.

The sector's overall goal is to increase access to education and training, improve the quality and relevance of education, reduce inequality, and leverage knowledge and skills in science, technology, and innovation for global competitiveness. The sector also envisions contributing to achieving the government agenda by providing the requisite skilled human resources and promoting research and development.

The budgetary allocation to Education sector in FY 2022/23 was Kshs.544.52 billion, revised to Kshs.567.04 billion in Supplementary Budget I, and Kshs.568.22 billion in Supplementary Budget II, compared to Kshs.527.28 billion allocated in FY 2021/22. The allocation to the Education sector represents 15.5 per cent of the revised gross National budget. The budget comprised Kshs.34.02 billion (6.0 per cent) for development activities and Kshs.534.20 billion (94.0 per cent) for recurrent expenditure.

The Teachers Service Commission (TSC) received the highest budgetary allocation at Kshs.300.20 billion (52.9 per cent of the Education sector's budget), while the State Department for Post Training and Skills Development had the lowest budgetary allocation at Kshs.129.36 million (less than 1 per cent of the Education sector allocation). TSC received the highest budgetary allocation of Kshs.300.20 billion (52.9 per cent of the sector's funding), which is attributed to its vital role in Teacher management for primary and secondary schools under Teacher Resource Management Programme.

In Supplementary Budget II, the State Department for Early Learning and Basic Education and the State Department for Vocational and Technical Training recorded the highest additional funding which was

towards Free Primary Education and Technical Trainers and Instructor Services respectively. The State Department for Early Learning and Basic Education's original gross estimates for the FY 2022/23 was Kshs.110.68 billion comprising Kshs.95.30 billion for recurrent expenditure and Kshs.15.38 billion for development expenditure.

heading_path: 4.5 Energy, Infrastructure, and Information Communications Technology (EI & ICT) Sector

blocks.text: This Sector consists of ten MDAs: State Departments for Infrastructure, Transport, Shipping and Maritime, Housing and Urban Development, Public Works, Information Communication, Technology, and Innovation, Broadcasting and Telecommunications, Ministry of Energy, Ministry of Petroleum and Mining, and the State Department for Mining.

The EI&ICT sector aims to provide an efficient, affordable, and reliable infrastructure critical for the socio-economic transformation underscored in the Third Medium Term Plan (MTP III) 2018-2022 of the Kenya Vision 2030 and catalyses the realisation of the government's agenda.

The EI&ICT sector's critical strategic goals include sustainable transport infrastructure and services, vibrant shipping and maritime industry, affordable and sustainable housing infrastructure, a regulated construction industry, universal access to ICT services, and sufficient, secure, efficient, and affordable energy.

4.6 Environmental Protection, Water, and Natural Resources (EPW&NR) Sector
heading_path: 4.6 Environmental Protection, Water, and Natural Resources (EPW&NR) Sector

blocks.text: The Environmental Protection, Water, and Natural Resources Sector (EPW&NR) comprises the Ministry of Environment and Forestry, the Ministry of Water, Sanitation and Irrigation, and the State Department for Wildlife.

The EPW&NR sector plays a critical role in Kenya's economy, securing, stewarding, and sustaining the environment and natural capital of the country. The overall goal of the EPW&NR sector is to ensure sustainable development in a clean and secure environment. The specific objectives include: providing the policy, the legal and integrated planning framework for sustainable management of the environment and natural resources for socio-economic development, enhancing good governance in the protection, restoration, conservation, development, and management of the environment, and forest resources for sustainable development, enhance control and development of water resources for sustainable social-economic development and to enhance water harvesting and storage for domestic, irrigation and industrial use. The sector also aims to increase land productivity through reclamation, rehabilitate degraded land through irrigation and drainage services, and enhance conversation of wildlife, biological resources, and their habitats for posterity.

The annual budgetary allocation to the EPW&NR sector in FY 2022/23 was Kshs.107.18 billion, revised to Kshs.87.7 billion in Supplementary Budget I and Kshs.95.63 billion in Supplementary Budget II, compared to 102.12 billion allocated in FY 2021/22. The allocation to the EPW&NR sector represents 2.6 per cent of the revised gross National budget. The budget comprised Kshs.68.00 billion (71.1 per cent) for development activities and Kshs.27.63 billion (28.9 per cent) for recurrent expenditure. The Ministry of Water and Sanitation and Irrigation received the highest budgetary allocation at Kshs.66.61 billion (69.6 per cent of the EPW&NR sector's budget), while the State Department for Irrigation had the lowest budgetary allocation at Kshs.2.58 billion (2.7 per cent of the EPW&NR sector allocation). The high allocation to the Ministry of Water and Sanitation and Irrigation is due to its critical roles including increasing agricultural productivity through irrigation and drainage services; development of water and sewerage infrastructure; and increasing the availability of safe and adequate water.

During the FY 2022/23, two Votes were created during the budget revision under EPW&NR Sector i.e. the State Department for Irrigation with an allocation of Kshs.2.58 billion; and the State Department for Forestry with an allocation of Kshs.3.01 billion. The State Department for Irrigation purposes to attain universal access to adequate, safe and sustainably managed water resources, sanitation and irrigation. The State Department for Forestry is tasked with promoting and facilitating a clean healthy, safe and sustainably managed environment and natural resources.

blocks.text: 4.6.4   Key Achievements for the EWP&NR Sector
heading_path: 4.6.4   Key Achievements for the EWP&NR Sector

blocks.text: The State Department for Wildlife, under the Wildlife Security Conservation and Management SubProgramme, responded to 980 clinical interventions for sick and injured wildlife animals out of 982 reported cases. The State Department also restored wildlife habitat through tree planting of 127,630 seedlings. In addition, the number of park visitors recorded was 2.4 million against a target of 2.1 million v, with the performance attributed to the recovery of the tourism sector. Following the increase in park visitors, a total of Kshs.5.24 billion in revenue was raised, surpassing the set target of Kshs.2.2 billion. Under the Wildlife Research and Training Sub-Programme, the State Department carried out four wildlife census reports, including lion census in Tsavo, marine mega fauna along the Kenyan Coast, Sable antelopes in Shimba Hills National Reserve, hippos in Lake Nakuru and Naivasha, and waterfalls in the Rift Valley.

blocks.text: The Ministry of Water, Sanitation, and Irrigation, through the Nairobi Rivers Basin Restoration Delivery Unit that is under the Water Resources Conservation and Protection Sub-Programme completed 70 per cent of Kasarani Mwiki and 73 per cent of Nairobi East West Reticulation sewers and 57 per cent of Kahawa West, Githurai Kahawa Sukari Reticulation of sewers against set targets of 60 per cent, 60 per cent and 50 per cent respectively. Under Kisumu Water Supply, the Ministry completed the water supply and sewerage infrastructure development project and is operational. Under the Sewerage Infrastructure Development Sub-Programme, the Ministry reported 64 per cent access to water services for the Lake Victoria South Works Development Agency. Under the Sewerage Infrastructure Development Sub-Programme, the Ministry drilled 42 exploratory boreholes in Kitui, Kajiado and Oloitoktok against a set target of 47 boreholes.

4.7 General	Economic	and	Commercial	Affairs	(GECA)	Sector
heading_path: 4.7 General	Economic	and	Commercial	Affairs	(GECA)	Sector

blocks.text: The General Economic and Commercial Affairs (GECA) sector consists of seven MDAs: The State Departments for Industrialization, Tourism, Trade and Enterprise Development, East African Community, Investment Promotion, Regional and Northern Corridor Development, and Micro Small and Medium Enterprises Development.

The GECA sector's strategic goals are aligned towards the promotion and development of domestic and regional trade, regional integration, industrialization, investment promotion, MSMES, tourism and regional integration and development.

The budgetary allocation to the GECA sector in FY 2022/23 was Kshs.26.03 billion, revised to Kshs.27.58 billion in Supplementary Budget I and Kshs.29.08 billion in Supplementary Budget II, compared to Kshs.25.56 billion allocated in FY 2021/22. The allocation to the GECA sector represents 0.8 per cent of the revised gross National budget. The budget comprised Kshs.7.73 billion (26.6 per cent) for development activities and Kshs.21.36 billion (73.4 per cent) for recurrent expenditure. The State

Department for Tourism received the highest budgetary allocation at Kshs.10.11 billion (34.8 per cent of the GECA sector's budget), while the State Department for Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development had the lowest budgetary allocation at Kshs.633.62 million (2.2 per cent of the GECA sector allocation).

The high allocation to the State Department for Tourism is due to the Tourism Product Development and Diversification Programme geared towards improving tourist destination competitiveness. The programme also encompasses the following sub-programmes: Niche Tourism Product Development and Diversification, Tourism Infrastructure Development, and Tourism Training and Capacity Building.

Following the reorganization of Government through Executive Order No.1 of 2022, additional Votes were created under the GECA Sector through the Supplementary Budget which include the State Department for Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development with an allocation of Kshs.633.62 million; and the State Department for Investment Promotion with an allocation of Kshs.2.16 billion. The State Department for Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development is tasked with creating an integrated enabling environment for a highly productive and diversified MSME Sector.

In Supplementary Budget II, the State Department for Trade and Enterprise Development and the State Department for Tourism recorded the highest additional funding, which was towards Domestic Trade and Enterprise Development (Kshs.486.10 million), Tourism Promotion Marketing (Kshs.31.77 million) and Tourism Product Development and Diversification (Kshs.300.00 million). The State Department for Trade and Enterprise Development's original gross estimates for the FY 2022/23 was Kshs.3.69 billion, comprising Kshs.2.42 billion for recurrent expenditure and Kshs.1.27 billion for development expenditure. This was revised to Kshs.4.22 billion in Supplementary II, comprising recurrent expenditure of Kshs.2.95 billion and development expenditure of Kshs.1.27 billion. The overall change reflects an increase of Kshs.529.40 million entirely for recurrent expenditure on account of enhanced A-I-A for Kenya National Trading Corporation and Weights & Measures Department and additional funding of Kshs.44.7 million on rent and parking arrears.

The State Department for Tourism's original gross estimates for the FY 2022/23 was Kshs.9.79 billion, comprising Kshs.9.76 billion for recurrent expenditure and Kshs.34.01 million for development expenditure. This was revised to Kshs.10.11 billion in Supplementary Budget II, of which recurrent expenditure was Kshs.10.05 billion and development expenditure to Kshs.59.01 million. This reflects an overall increase of Kshs.322.00 million, comprising an additional Kshs.297.00 million in the recurrent expenditure and an additional Kshs.25.00 million in development expenditure. The increase of Kshs.322 million was due to Kshs.30 million additional funding for the royal tour documentary and enhanced AIA by Kshs.300 million for the Tourism Fund.

blocks.text: The State Department of East African Community (EAC) implemented several activities across the EAC integration pillars: EAC Customs Union, EAC Common Market, EAC Monetary Union and EAC Political Federation. The EAC Common Market participated in the National High-Level Dialogue on Domestic Resource Mobilization for Sustainable Health Financing towards Universal Health Coverage in June 2023. Further, they participated in harmonising EAC Partner States Education and Training Curricula, Examination Structures and Frameworks for Certification and Accreditation. This facilitates the mobility of staff and students across the EAC Partner States and creates employment for staff and TVET graduates.

4.8 Governance, Justice, Law and Order (GJLO) Sector
heading_path: 4.8 Governance, Justice, Law and Order (GJLO) Sector

blocks.text: The GJLO Sector consists of seventeen MDAs, which include the State Department for Interior and Citizen Services, the State Department for Correctional Services, State Department for Immigration and Citizen Services, National Police Service, State Department for Internal Security and National

Administration, the State Law Office and Department of Justice, The Judiciary, Ethics and AntiCorruption Commission (EACC), the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions (ODPP), Office of the Registrar of Political Parties (ORPP), Witness Protection Agency (WPA), Kenya National Commission on Human Rights (KNCHR), Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC), Judicial Service Commission (JSC), National Police Service Commission (NPSC), National Gender and Equality Commission (NGEC), and the Independent Policing Oversight Authority (IPOA) as well as SAGAs and Tribunals under the Judiciary.

The GJLO Sector creates a favourable environment for the country's economic, social, and political development necessary for fulfilling the objectives of the Kenya Vision 2030. It comprises institutions with linkages in peace and security building, correctional services, legal advisory services to government agencies, National government representation in civil proceedings and matters before foreign courts and tribunals, and dispensation of justice. The GJLO Sector also significantly promotes good governance, integrity, and corruption eradication, provides public prosecution services, regulates political parties, and protects witnesses and human rights. Further, the sector also delimits electoral boundaries and manages electoral processes, promoting gender equality, including marginalised groups and communities, and oversight of police operations.

Besides, GJLO Sector plays a role in border management, peace-building and conflict management, registration services, gaming industry regulation, population management services, eradicating drugs and substance abuse, crime research, and government printing services. The Sector also plays a crucial role in ensuring National values and promoting National cohesion.

The budgetary allocation to the GJLO Sector in FY 2022/23 was Kshs.234.41 billion, revised to Kshs.239.51 billion in Supplementary Budget I, and Kshs.240.88 billion in Supplementary Budget II, compared to Kshs.233.12 billion allocated in FY 2021/22. The allocation to the GJLO sector represents 6.6 per cent of the revised gross National budget. The budget comprised Kshs.6.82 billion (2.8 per cent) for development activities and Kshs.234.06 billion (97.2 per cent) for recurrent expenditure. The State Department for Interior and Citizen Services received the highest budgetary allocation at Kshs.112.09 billion (46.1 per cent of the GJLO sector's budget), while the State Department for National Gender & Equality Commission had the lowest budgetary allocation at Kshs.408.38 million (less than 1 per cent of the GJLO sector allocation).

The high allocation to the State Department for Interior and Citizen Services is due its roles including enhancing public safety and security; provision of migration and citizen services; population management services; and the production and security of Government documents.

During the FY 2022/23, the following Votes were established during the budget revision under GJLO Sector: State Department for Immigration and Citizen Services with an allocation of Kshs.2.01 billion; National Police Service with an allocation of Kshs.25.18 billion; and State Department for Internal Security and National Administration with and allocation of Kshs.8.85 billion. The three Votes were previously domiciled under the State Department for Interior and Citizen Services. The State Department for Immigration is tasked with maintaining a comprehensive population database, proper migration management and timely registration and issuance of secure identification documents. The National Police Services aims to provide a professional, innovative and people-centred police service.

The State Department for Internal Security and National Administration is tasked with the provision of security and safety to people and property, promotion of National cohesion and coordination of National government functions

blocks.text: 4.8.4  Key Achievements for the GJLO Sector
heading_path: 4.8.4  Key Achievements for the GJLO Sector

blocks.text: In FY 2022/23, the Ethics and Anti-Corruption Commission received adequate support from the National Treasury to discharge its mandate. As a result, some significant achievements included completing 296 investigation files on corruption and economic crimes were forwarded to the Director of Public Prosecution. Further, they conducted 39 proactive covert investigations, averting possible loss of public funds estimated at Kshs.7.33 billion.
heading_path: 4.8.4  Key Achievements for the GJLO Sector

blocks.text: The Judiciary established operational instruments that enabled the operationalization of the Judiciary Fund. This aimed at ensuring financial independence to the Judiciary as envisaged by the Kenyan constitution. The Judiciary heard and determined the Presidential petition within the 14 days stipulated in the Constitution. Other petitions for Governors, Senators, Members of Parliament, and Members of the County Assembly are at various levels of the court. In addition, the Judiciary conducted admission of over 1000 Advocates, establishment of the first special Sexual and Gender Based Violence Court in Shanzu Law Court and operationalized six magistrate court Stations; Kenol, Rumuruti, Olkalou, Tinderet, Kabiyet and Madiany.
heading_path: 4.8.4  Key Achievements for the GJLO Sector

blocks.text: The National Police Service was created as a new vote effective 1st April 2023 and by the end of the financial 2022/23, it had procured new enhanced Medical Insurance Cover and Group Life Insurance Cover for all officers in the National Police Service.
heading_path: 4.8.4  Key Achievements for the GJLO Sector

blocks.text: The Independent Policing Oversight Authority continued its mandate of police accountability through various police operations, such as conducting investigations. As a result, they investigated and finalized 876 cases and made multiple recommendations, including prosecution and disciplinary action, in line with the Independent Policing Oversight Authority Act of 2011. Furthermore, the Authority conducted 762 inspections, monitored 122 police operations, and finalized the review and approval of IPOA Regulations to guide the implementation of the IPOA Act.

Health is a devolved function under the Fourth Schedule of the Constitution of Kenya. At the National level Health sector is responsible for providing and coordinating health policy formulation, ensuring quality service delivery, and regulating health care.

The Health sector comprises of Ministry of Health, State Department for Public Health and Professional Standards, and Semi-Autonomous Government Agencies, namely: Kenyatta National Hospital, Moi Teaching and Referral Hospital, Kenya Medical Research Institute, Kenya Medical Supplies Authority, Kenya Medical Training College, National Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome (AIDS) Control Council, Kenyatta University Teaching, Referral and Research Hospital, National Cancer Institute of Kenya, Kenya Nuclear Regulatory Authority and the National Health Insurance Fund.

The budgetary allocation to the Health sector in FY 2022/23 was Kshs.122.52 billion, revised to Kshs.119.37 billion in Supplementary Budget I, and Kshs.116.40 billion in Supplementary Budget II, compared to Kshs.121.09 billion allocated in FY 2021/22. The allocation to the sector represents 3.2 per cent of the revised gross National budget. The budget comprised Kshs.44.32 billion (38.1 per cent) for development activities and Kshs.72.07 billion (61.9 per cent) for recurrent expenditure.

The Ministry of Health received the highest budgetary allocation at Kshs.111.17 billion (95.5 per cent of the Health sector's budget), while the State Department for Public Health and Professional Standards receivedKshs.5.21 billion (4.5 per cent of the Health sector allocation). The State Department for Public Health and Professional Standards Vote was created through Executive Order No.1 of 2022 and allocated funds through supplementary budget. The Vote is tasked with building a progressive and sustainable health care system for accelerated attainment of the highest standard of health for all Kenyans.

blocks.text: 4.9.4  Key Achievements for the Health Sector
heading_path: 4.9.4  Key Achievements for the Health Sector

blocks.text: The Health Sector achievements for FY 2022/23 were based on the planned outputs and services to be delivered to the citizens per the budget allocations.
heading_path: 4.9.4  Key Achievements for the Health Sector

blocks.text: In the period under review, the preventive and promotive programmes identified 1.3 million people living with HIV and initiated antiretroviral treatment representing a coverage of 87 per cent. Under the same programme, Immunization coverage improved from 84 per cent in FY 2020/21 to 88 per cent in FY 2021/22 due to the procurement and installation of specialized vaccine storage equipment in over 3,500 health facilities and 290 sub-County vaccine depots.
heading_path: 4.9.4  Key Achievements for the Health Sector

blocks.text: The programme also distributed 16 million Long-Lasting Insecticidal Nets across 27 Counties. This has benefited approximately 26 million persons and seen a drop in the prevalence of malaria infections from 8 per cent to 6 per cent. The sector also continued with the vitamin A supplementation programme for children ages 6 to 59 months. As of the close of FY 2022/23, they attained 86.3 per cent, surpassing the global and National target of 80 per cent.
heading_path: 4.9.4  Key Achievements for the Health Sector

blocks.text: The sector established 19 County-based cancer registries, an increase from 12 established in the FY 2020/21; 58 cancer treatment centres met the minimum standards of cancer centre care, 10 regional chemotherapy centres and three radiotherapy centres were fully established in Nakuru, Garissa, and Mombasa each being equipped with a state-of-the-art linear accelerator, Computed Tomography simulator and brachytherapy machine.

blocks.text: 4.11 Public Administration and International Relations (PAIR) Sector
heading_path: 4.11 Public Administration and International Relations (PAIR) Sector

blocks.text: The Sector provides National leadership, oversight, and policy direction towards the realization of the country's development agenda. It promotes prudent public finance management and accountability in the Public Sector; coordinates National and sectoral development planning; oversees an efficient and effective Public Service. It also coordinates Kenya's foreign policy and diaspora affairs, wage bill  management, development of a sound legislative and regulatory framework, and enforces administrative justice and the right to information.

Following the reorganization of the government after the general elections in August 2022 and further directives by H.E President of the Republic of Kenya, some Ministries in PAIR sector were split and new MDAs created. The PAIR sector comprises of twenty MDAs , namely, the Executive Office of the President; Office of the Deputy President; State Department for Cabinet Affairs; State Department for Devolution; State Department for Performance and Delivery Management; State Department for Parliamentary Affairs; State Department for Foreign Affairs; State Department for Diaspora Affairs; The National Treasury; State Department for Economic Planning; State Department for Public Service; Parliamentary Service Commission; National Assembly; Parliamentary Joint Services; Commission on Revenue Allocation; Public Service Commission; Salaries and Remuneration Commission; Office of the Auditor General; Office of the Controller of Budget; and Commission on Administrative Justice
4.11.2  Budget Performance for the PAIR Sector
heading_path: 4.11.2  Budget Performance for the PAIR Sector

blocks.text: The budgetary allocation to the PAIR sector in FY 2022/23 amounted to Kshs.356.86 billion, revised to Kshs.358.41 billion in Supplementary Budget I and Kshs.345.14 billion in Supplementary Budget II, compared to Kshs.358.30 billion allocated in FY 2021/22. The allocation to the Pair sector represents 9.4 per cent of the revised gross National budget. The budget comprised Kshs146.66 billion (42.5 per cent) for development activities and Kshs.198.48 billion (57.5 per cent) for recurrent expenditure. The National Treasury received the highest budgetary allocation at Kshs.147.56 billion (42.7 per cent of the PAIR sector's budget), while the State Department for Salaries and Remuneration Commission had the lowest budgetary allocation at Kshs.504.9 million (less than 1 per cent of the PAIR sector allocation).
heading_path: 4.11.2  Budget Performance for the PAIR Sector

blocks.text: The high allocation to the National Treasury is due to its vital role in ensuring a stable micro and macro-economic environment and promoting sustainable market competition.
heading_path: 4.11.2  Budget Performance for the PAIR Sector

blocks.text: In Supplementary Budget II, the President's Executive Office received the highest additional funding for Cabinet and State House Affairs. The State Department for Executive Office of the President's original gross estimates for the FY 2022/23 was Kshs.23.07 billion, comprising Kshs.17.08 billion for recurrent expenditure and Kshs.5.98 billion for development expenditure. This was been revised to Kshs.35.04 billion in Supplementary II, of which recurrent expenditure is Kshs.27.23 billion while development expenditure is Kshs.7.81 billion. The overall change reflects an increase in Kshs.11.97 billion, comprising an addition of Kshs.10.15 billion in the recurrent expenditure and an additional Kshs.1.83 billion in development expenditure. The change in the recurrent expenditure is due to facilitating effective cabinet decisions for harmonious operation in government and Execution of the President's mandate as per the Constitution.

4.12 Social Protection, Culture, and Recreation (SPCR) Sector
heading_path: 4.12 Social Protection, Culture, and Recreation (SPCR) Sector

blocks.text: The Social Protection, Culture, and Recreation Sector comprises the six MDAs: Sports, Culture and Heritage, Labour, Social Protection, Pensions and Senior Citizens Affairs, Development of Arid and Semi-Arid Lands (ASALs), and Gender.

The SPCR sector plays a strategic role in the country's transformation and socio-economic development by implementing special programmes for the development of the ASALs. The SPCR sector promotes sustainable employment, harmonious industrial relations, a productive workforce, and gender equity

and equality. Other key roles include empowering communities and vulnerable groups, safeguarding children's rights, and promoting diverse cultures, arts, and sports to enhance cohesiveness and Kenya's regional and international competitiveness.

The budgetary allocation to the SPCR sector in FY 2022/23 was Kshs.73.21 billion, revised to Kshs.82.81 billion in Supplementary Budget I and and Kshs.83.57 billion in Supplementary Budget II, compared to Kshs.75.03 billion allocated in FY 2021/22. The allocation to the SPCR sector represents 2.3 per cent of the revised gross National budget. The budget comprised Kshs.33.0 billion (39.5 per cent) for development activities and Kshs.50.57 billion (60.5 per cent) for recurrent expenditure.

The State Department for Social Protection, Pensions and Senior Citizens Affairs received the highest budgetary allocation at Kshs.38.25 billion (45.8 per cent of the SPCR sector's budget), while the State Department for Culture and Heritage had the lowest budgetary allocation at Kshs.3.30 billion (3.9 per cent of the SPCR sector allocation). The high allocation to the State Department for Social Protection, Pensions and Senior Citizens Affairs is due its role in promoting and coordinating community empowerment, care, participation, and protection of children, persons with disabilities and other vulnerable groups as an integral part of National development.

This chapter highlights the critical issues that affected budget implementation in FY 2022/23 and provides recommendations for effective budget execution.
During the year, the Controller of Budget identified critical issues that affected budget implementation as discussed hereunder:

As of 30th June 2023, the public debt stock stood at Ksh.10.25 trillion from Kshs.8.63 trillion reported on 30th June 2022. The National Treasury paid off Kshs.543.95 billion of loan principal, Kshs.607.28 billion as interest, Kshs.1.36 billion in commitment fees, and Kshs.536.85 million in penalties and other charges.

The country has a significant amount of public debt denominated in foreign currencies, which makes it vulnerable to currency fluctuations and exchange rate risks. The exchange rate between the Kenya Shilling and the US Dollar was roughly 117.87 Kenya shillings in July 2022, while in June 2023, it averaged 141.14, a difference of 23.27 shillings (approximately 18.9 per cent exchange rate depreciation). The depreciation of the Kenyan Shilling caused an increase in the debt stock and debt repayments (principal and interest) in Kenya Shilling terms. The continuous depreciation of the Kenya Shilling will necessitate an increase in the amount required for loan repayments. This will erode the government's fiscal space and limit the implementation of other critical policies and programs, resulting in budget adjustments.

The Controller of Budget recommends a special audit of existing and committed loans to link the loans with the projects funded through borrowed funds. Further, the office observed that the National Treasury has, over the years, acquired and absorbed loans on behalf of profitable Semi-Autonomous Government Agencies. These loans should be reviewed with the aim of transferring payment obligations to the Agencies.

An analysis of domestic debt shows that investors preferred the shorter 91-day Treasury Bills, which is attributed to avoidance of duration risk. On several occasions, the Government could not raise adequate funds on the domestic market from Treasury Bonds, signaling an avoidance of long-term lending by investors.

Shorter-term maturity loans are more expensive and pressure revenue as a more significant proportions of the collected income is committed to debt servicing. The public debt payment is a first charge on the Consolidated Fund; and thus, inadequate collections from Treasury Bonds imply increased debt payments on Treasury Bill redemptions at the expense of the recurrent and development expenditures.

The Controller of Budget recommends fiscal consolidation to enhance fiscal discipline. Further, revenue measures, such as enhanced efficiency in tax administration to eliminate tax evasion, improve tax
compliance, widen the tax base and ensure government subsidies are aimed at supporting production for higher economic growth.

As of 30th June 2023, the total pending bills of the National and County governments stood at Ksh.727.74 billion, consisting of Kshs.567.50 billion and Kshs.160.24billion for the National and County governments, respectively.

The Controller of Budget takes cognizance of the establishment of a Special Committee on the verification of pending bills by the Cabinet on 27th June 2023. The Committee was tasked with auditing liabilities for the period between 2005 and 2022 and consists of members from the Attorney General's Office, the State Department of Roads, the State Department of Public Works, the State Department of Housing and Urban Development and the Public Procurement Regulatory Authority. The Committee, however does not include critical institutions in public finance management such as the Controller of Budget, Office of the Auditor General, the National Treasury and County Treasuries.
The Controller of Budget recommends consideration for the inclusion of crucial institutions in public finance management in the pending bills verification committee to enhance its effectiveness.

Analysis of financial and non-financial reports submitted to the Controller of Budget shows that some MDAs' economic items and sub-programmes exceeded the budget and reflected negative balances and over-absorption of funds. Section 43 of the Public Finance Management Act specifies clear guidelines on budget reallocation.

The Controller of Budget recommends that Accounting Officers adhere to Section 43 of the PFM Act and ensure reallocated budget items are regularised in the consequent Supplementary Budget. For best practices, there is a need to identify budget lines and programmes/sub-programmes that are not likely to be utilised and reallocation to those likely to utilise the budget fully.

This National Government Budget Implementation Review Report was prepared to fulfil Article 228 of the Constitution of Kenya and Section 9 of the Controller of Budget Act, 2016. It provides financial and non-financial information on budget performance in FY 2022/23 and also identifies the key issues that hampered effective budget execution during the year.

The period under review was mainly marked by a transition in government administration following the August 2022 general elections, which occasioned Government reorganisation. The National Government MDAs were increased from 68 Votes to 81 in line with Executive Order Number 1 of 2022. There was also an observable shift in allocations within Sectors and MDAs, indicating a change in government priorities and policy direction. The revised gross budget for FY 2022/23 was Kshs.4.18 trillion compared to Kshs.4 trillion for FY 2021/22. It comprised of Kshs.3.67 trillion and Kshs.515.18 billion for the National and County governments, respectively.

Receipts into the Consolidated Fund were Kshs.3.24 trillion, representing 89.6 per cent of the revised annual target compared to Kshs.3.06 trillion received in FY 2021/22 (91.7 per cent of the annual target). This increase is attributed to increased tax-revenue targets and observable focus on external loans and grants funding. The total exchequer issues in the financial year were Kshs.3.27 trillion, representing 87.6 per cent of the revised net estimates, comprised of Kshs.308.03 billion for development expenditure, Kshs.2.54 trillion for recurrent expenditure, and Kshs.399.60 billion for County governments, representing 82.4 per cent, 89.1 per cent, and 100 per cent, respectively. The failure to fund 12.3 per cent of the budget affected the attainment of several planned activities and interrupted service delivery to the citizens.

Total expenditure for the National government was Kshs.3.18 trillion, representing an overall budget absorption rate of 86.6 per cent, compared to the 85.4 per cent (Kshs.2.96 trillion) achieved in FY 2021/22. This comprised of development expenditure of Kshs.473.55 billion, an absorption rate of 81.3 per cent, recurrent expenditure of Kshs.2.71 trillion, representing 87.6 per cent of the revised recurrent gross budget. Recurrent expenditure consisted of Kshs.1.40 trillion (absorption rate 92.8 per cent) and Kshs.1.31 trillion (absorption rate 82.7 per cent) for MDAs and Consolidated Fund Services, respectively.

The Controller of Budget observed several challenges that hampered budget implementation in FY 2022/23. They include the rise in public debt service cost occasioned by the increase in the Country's public debt stock, liquidity constraints and an increase in pending bills.

To address the challenges, the Controller of Budget recommends a special audit of the existing loans and committed loans, which will link the loans with the projects funded through borrowed funds; the National Treasury should also explore opportunities of accessing funding in multiple currencies to guard against intense pressure on the local currency. There is a need for fiscal consolidation with a target to reduce deficit budget financing and focus on tax administration measures to boost revenue collection.
